title: Watermarking Game-Playing Agents in Perfect-Information Extensive-Form Games
claim: Watermarked agents show steadily growing detection statistics and strong ROC separability, while unwatermarked originals stay near zero across all engines.
layout: 3 panels in a row, line plots; solid vs dotted lines, shared engine legend
description: Three side-by-side line plots share one color-per-engine scheme (six chess engines, legend at far right). The left plot shows z-score versus round (0 to 100), and the middle plot shows z-score versus number of moves excluding book moves (0 to about 10,000). In both, solid watermarked curves climb from near 0 to between about 19 and 47, with Dragon (orange) highest. Dotted curves for the original engines stay flat near 0. The right plot shows ROC curves, with true positive rate against false positive rate and a dashed diagonal chance line. All engine curves bow well above the diagonal. The eye goes first to the orange curve rising far above the cluster of flat dotted lines.
caption: On the left and in the middle, respectively, the z-scores over the number of rounds and moves, respectively. On the right, the ROC curves for watermark detection (for each round). Solid and dotted lines, respectively, represent watermarked and original chess engines, respectively. The AUC values of the ROC curves are tabulated in Table [ref].
abstract: Watermarking techniques for large language models (LLMs), which encode hidden information in the output so its source can be verified, have gained significant attention in recent days, thanks to their potential capability to detect accidental or deliberate misuse. Similar challenges involving model misuse also exist in the context of game-playing, such as when detecting the unauthorized use of AI tools in gaming platforms (e.g., cheating in online chess). In this paper, we initiate the study of how game-playing strategies can be watermarked. We show how the KGW watermark for LLMs can be adapted to watermark game-playing agents in perfect-information extensive-form games. The watermark can then be detected using a statistical test. We show that the degradation in the quality of the watermarked strategy profile, quantified by the expected utility, can be bounded, but there is a tradeoff between detectability and quality. In our experiments, we bootstrap the watermarking framework to various chess engines and demonstrate that a) the impact of the watermark on the quality of the strategy is negligible and b) the watermark can be detected with just a handful of games.
